To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dietary reporting groups can cause selection bias, and that the use of external predictors of dietary reporting can be used to correct misreported data.
dietary under-reporting is a common phenomenon in adolescents and that it can be corrected by using external predictors of under-reporting.

(1) fat-free mass (FFM) is a valid predictor of energy intake (EI); (2) FFM is a valid predictor for the misreporting of EI; (3) the association between FFM and EI is stronger in plausible reporters than in other reporters; and (4) the association between EI and FFM is stronger in plausible EI reporters when the sample is restricted to plausible reporters.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the problem of under-reporting in dietary surveys.
the question of whether the energy intake (EI) of adolescents can be estimated by means of self-reported dietary intake data (sEI), which are usually obtained from dietary questionnaires.
the question of whether the subjective energy intake (sIE) of adolescents is related to their body composition.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the association between sEI data and body composition is stronger when sEI data are adjusted for common predictors of mis-reporting, such as BMI, restraint, physical activity or fat mass.
misreporting can indeed be corrected, but it should not be done by restricting data to plausible reporters, but by statistically controlling for the predictors of misreport.
misreporting of dietary data can be corrected by statistically controlling for dietary misreporting groups and/or statistically controlling for predictors of dietary misreporting.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the association between sEI data and fat-free mass can be corrected by statistically controlling for dietary misreporting.
dietary reporting groups are useful in identifying misreporting and in excluding implausible data.
the association between energy consumption and fat-free mass is robust, but the association with energy expenditure is not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
researchers should not use sEI data without correction.
misreported sEI can be corrected, and that statistical methods that do not correct for sEI misreport are likely to underestimate the strength of the association between sEI data and health outcomes.
researchers should be aware that statistical correction for sEI misreport can be a powerful method to correct for selection bias.
